Introduction to connectedness

Source: vignettes/intro.Rmd
intro.Rmd

What problem does this package solve?

In genetic evaluation, animals are often compared across herds, flocks, regions, years, or other management units (MUs). Those comparisons are not equally reliable in all data sets. When management units are weakly linked by pedigree or genomic relationships, differences in estimated breeding values across units become less precise.

The connectedness package computes pairwise connectedness between MUs from the same ingredients that define the evaluation context:

  • the relationship structure among animals,
  • the assignment of animals to management units,
  • the fixed-effects design,
  • and the assumed variance components.

The package supports connectedness computed from:

  • A-inverse (pedigree-based connectedness),
  • G-inverse (genomic connectedness),
  • H-inverse (combined pedigree-genomic connectedness), and
  • a custom inverse kernel supplied by the user.

Which metrics does the package compute?

The package reports two complementary contrast-based metrics:

  • PEVD contrast: prediction error variance of differences between MU contrasts. Lower values indicate stronger connectedness.
  • CD contrast: coefficient of determination for the same contrasts. Higher values indicate stronger connectedness.

Both metrics are computed through mixed model equations (MME). The package uses the relationship kernel and the fixed-effect structure to evaluate the precision of pairwise MU contrasts, not a separate heuristic summary.

If desired, PEVD can be returned scaled by the additive genetic variance by setting scale_pevd = TRUE in compute_connectedness().

What are target animals?

The target animals are the animals that receive non-zero weights in the pairwise contrast vector. They are not necessarily the only animals used in the mixed-model equations. Other animals may contribute information through their records and relationships, but receive zero weight in a specific MU contrast.

This distinction is especially important when a time window is used. The MME can be built using all records in data, while CD/PEVD are reported for contrasts among a temporally defined set of target animals.

For a pair of MUs, target animals from one MU receive weights 1 / n_i, target animals from the other MU receive weights -1 / n_j, and all other animals receive weight zero in that contrast. Those zero-weight animals can still affect the solution through relationships and records in the MME.

Quick start

For most users, the main entry point is compute_connectedness().

A minimal pedigree-based analysis looks like this:

library(connectedness)

res <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ainv",
  pedigree      = pedigree
)

print(res)
plot(res, which = "CD")
plot(res, which = "PEVD")

The short workflow is:

  1. provide animals, MUs, and fixed effects,
  2. choose the relationship representation,
  3. obtain pairwise CD and PEVD between reported MUs.

Inputs: what does the function need?

The package separates the problem into two layers.

Evaluation context

These inputs define the comparison problem:

  • data: records used to define animals, MUs, and fixed effects,
  • animal_col: animal identifier column,
  • mu_col: management-unit column,
  • fixed_formula: fixed-effects structure,
  • sigma2a, sigma2e: variance components.

Relationship structure

These inputs define how animals are connected genetically:

  • relationship = "Ainv" requires a pedigree,
  • relationship = "Ginv" requires a genotype matrix X and an index linking row order to animal IDs,
  • relationship = "Hinv" requires pedigree + genotypes + genotyped_idx,
  • relationship = "custom" uses a supplied inverse kernel.

Outputs: what do you get back?

compute_connectedness() returns an object of class "connectedness". The most important components are:

  • CD: matrix of pairwise CD contrast values,
  • PEVD: matrix of pairwise PEVD contrast values,
  • qK: denominator of the contrast under the chosen kernel,
  • qC: prediction error numerator of the contrast,
  • n_target: number of target animals per reported MU,
  • report_mus: MUs included in the reported CD/PEVD matrices,
  • target_scope: definition of the target animals used in the contrasts,
  • relationship: inverse relationship matrix type used,
  • activity_summary: temporal MU activity summary when a time window and min_records_per_year are used,
  • overlap: temporal overlap table when a time window is used.

When a time window is used, n_target refers to animals receiving non-zero weights in the contrast. It does not necessarily include all animals used in the MME.

If scale_pevd = TRUE, the PEVD matrix is returned on the scale PEVD / sigma2a.

Example: weak vs strong connectedness

The example below contrasts two small pedigree scenarios:

  • a weakly connected setting, where the two MUs are linked only weakly,
  • a more connected setting, where a sire is shared across MUs.

The goal is not biological realism, but to illustrate how the package responds to a simple change in pedigree structure.

Scenario 1: weaker connectedness 

pedigree_weak <- data.frame(
  animal = c("S1", "S2", "D1", "D2", "A1", "A2", "B1", "B2"),
  sire   = c("0",  "0",  "0",  "0",  "S1", "S1", "S2", "S2"),
  dam    = c("0",  "0",  "0",  "0",  "D1", "D2", "D1", "D2")
)

data_weak <- data.frame(
  animal = c("A1", "A2", "B1", "B2"),
  MU     = c("MU1", "MU1", "MU2", "MU2"),
  sex    = c("M", "F", "M", "F")
)

res_weak <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_weak,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ainv",
  pedigree      = pedigree_weak
)

Scenario 2: stronger connectedness through a shared sire 

pedigree_strong <- data.frame(
  animal = c("S1", "D1", "D2", "A1", "A2", "B1", "B2"),
  sire   = c("0",  "0",  "0",  "S1", "S1", "S1", "S1"),
  dam    = c("0",  "0",  "0",  "D1", "D2", "D1", "D2")
)

data_strong <- data.frame(
  animal = c("A1", "A2", "B1", "B2"),
  MU     = c("MU1", "MU1", "MU2", "MU2"),
  sex    = c("M", "F", "M", "F")
)

res_strong <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ainv",
  pedigree      = pedigree_strong
)

Compare the two results 

res_weak$CD
res_weak$PEVD
res_weak$qK

res_strong$CD
res_strong$PEVD
res_strong$qK

The weak-versus-strong comparison is useful because PEVD and CD are related but not identical summaries. A stronger pedigree link can reduce PEVD, improving precision of the contrast. At the same time, the kernel-based denominator qK can also change because the MUs become less genetically distinct. CD is interpreted relative to that denominator.

Optional PEVD scaling 

res_strong_scaled <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ainv",
  pedigree      = pedigree_strong,
  scale_pevd    = TRUE
)

res_strong_scaled$PEVD

Relationship structures

A practical way to think about the four options is:

  • use Ainv when the target notion of connectedness is pedigree-based,
  • use Ginv when realized genomic links are the main object of interest,
  • use Hinv when the connectedness measure should align with a combined pedigree-genomic evaluation context,
  • use custom when your inverse kernel is built elsewhere.

A-inverse 

res_A <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ainv",
  pedigree      = pedigree_strong
)

G-inverse 

X <- matrix(
  c(0, 1, 2, 1,
    1, 1, 2, 0,
    2, 1, 0, 1,
    1, 2, 1, 0),
  nrow = 4,
  byrow = TRUE
)
rownames(X) <- c("A1", "A2", "B1", "B2")

animal_index <- setNames(seq_len(nrow(X)), rownames(X))

res_G <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ginv",
  X             = X,
  animal_index  = animal_index
)

H-inverse 

renum <- renum_pedigree(pedigree_strong, verbose = FALSE)
genotyped_idx <- renum$new_id[match(rownames(X), renum$animal)]

res_H <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Hinv",
  pedigree      = pedigree_strong,
  X             = X,
  genotyped_idx = genotyped_idx
)

Custom inverse kernels

Custom inverse kernels are useful when the relationship inverse is built by external software or by a user-defined method. The key requirement is that row and column identifiers match the names of animal_index.

The example below exports a package-built Ainv as triplets, reads it back, and uses it through relationship = "custom".

library(Matrix)

renum <- renum_pedigree(pedigree_strong, verbose = FALSE)
Ainv_res <- build_Ainv(renum)
Ainv_custom <- Ainv_res$Ainv

animal_index_custom <- stats::setNames(renum$new_id, renum$animal)
animal_index_custom <- animal_index_custom[!is.na(names(animal_index_custom))]

Ainv_triplet <- summary(Ainv_custom)
idx_to_id <- names(animal_index_custom)[order(animal_index_custom)]

Ainv_triplet_out <- data.frame(
  row = idx_to_id[Ainv_triplet$i],
  col = idx_to_id[Ainv_triplet$j],
  value = Ainv_triplet$x
)

write.table(
  Ainv_triplet_out,
  file = "Ainv_custom_triplet.txt",
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = TRUE,
  quote = FALSE
)

Ainv_triplet_in <- read.table(
  "Ainv_custom_triplet.txt",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

i <- animal_index_custom[Ainv_triplet_in$row]
j <- animal_index_custom[Ainv_triplet_in$col]

Ainv_custom_in <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(
  i = i,
  j = j,
  x = Ainv_triplet_in$value,
  dims = c(length(animal_index_custom), length(animal_index_custom))
)

Ainv_custom_in <- Matrix::forceSymmetric(Ainv_custom_in, uplo = "L")
Ainv_custom_in <- methods::as(Ainv_custom_in, "dgCMatrix")

res_custom <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "custom",
  rel_matrix    = Ainv_custom_in,
  animal_index  = animal_index_custom
)

max(abs(res_A$CD - res_custom$CD), na.rm = TRUE)
max(abs(res_A$PEVD - res_custom$PEVD), na.rm = TRUE)

If a custom file stores only one triangle of a symmetric sparse matrix, the matrix must be symmetrized before calling compute_connectedness().

Using a time window to define target animals

A time window is used to select MUs of interest and, by default, to define the animals that receive non-zero weights in the contrast. The MME itself is still built from all records supplied in data.

target_scope MME uses Target animals Question answered
"window" all records in data animals from selected MUs inside year_window recent connectedness within the full system
"selected_mus" all records in data all animals from selected MUs accumulated connectedness of active MUs 
pedigree_time <- data.frame(
  animal = c("S1", "D1", "D2", "A0", "A1", "A2", "B0", "B1", "B2"),
  sire   = c("0",  "0",  "0",  "S1", "S1", "S1", "S1", "S1", "S1"),
  dam    = c("0",  "0",  "0",  "D1", "D1", "D2", "D1", "D1", "D2")
)

data_time <- data.frame(
  animal = c("A0", "A1", "A2", "B0", "B1", "B2"),
  MU     = c("MU1", "MU1", "MU1", "MU2", "MU2", "MU2"),
  sex    = c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M", "F"),
  year   = c(2015, 2020, 2021, 2015, 2020, 2021)
)

res_window <- compute_connectedness(
  data                 = data_time,
  animal_col           = "animal",
  mu_col               = "MU",
  fixed_formula        = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a              = 50,
  sigma2e              = 100,
  relationship         = "Ainv",
  pedigree             = pedigree_time,
  year_col             = "year",
  year_window          = c(2020, 2021),
  min_records_per_year = 1,
  target_scope         = "window"
)

res_selected_mus <- compute_connectedness(
  data                 = data_time,
  animal_col           = "animal",
  mu_col               = "MU",
  fixed_formula        = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a              = 50,
  sigma2e              = 100,
  relationship         = "Ainv",
  pedigree             = pedigree_time,
  year_col             = "year",
  year_window          = c(2020, 2021),
  min_records_per_year = 1,
  target_scope         = "selected_mus"
)

res_window$n_target
res_selected_mus$n_target

With target_scope = "window", the target animals are A1, A2, B1, and B2. With target_scope = "selected_mus", the target animals are A0, A1, A2, B0, B1, and B2.

Summarizing connectedness

The output matrices are pairwise. The helpers below summarize those pairwise values; they do not create new contrasts against “all other MUs”.

Overall pairwise summaries 

overall_connectedness <- function(res) {
  up <- upper.tri(res$CD)

  data.frame(
    n_mus = nrow(res$CD),
    n_pairs = sum(up),
    mean_CD = mean(res$CD[up], na.rm = TRUE),
    median_CD = stats::median(res$CD[up], na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_PEVD = mean(res$PEVD[up], na.rm = TRUE),
    median_PEVD = stats::median(res$PEVD[up], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

overall_connectedness(res_strong)

MU-level summaries 

mu_connectedness_summary <- function(res) {
  CD <- res$CD
  PEVD <- res$PEVD

  diag(CD) <- NA_real_
  diag(PEVD) <- NA_real_

  data.frame(
    MU = rownames(CD),
    mean_CD_to_others = rowMeans(CD, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_CD_to_others = apply(CD, 1, stats::median, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_PEVD_to_others = rowMeans(PEVD, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_PEVD_to_others = apply(PEVD, 1, stats::median, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_target = res$n_target[rownames(CD)]
  )
}

mu_connectedness_summary(res_strong)

Visualization

The package provides a direct plotting method for a first visual inspection.

plot(res_strong, which = "CD")
plot(res_strong, which = "PEVD")
plot(res_strong, which = "all")
plot(res_window, which = "overlap")

A quick visual check is often the easiest way to identify MU pairs that are well connected, weakly connected, or effectively isolated.

Computational notes

For large analyses, first inspect the problem size without solving:

diag <- compute_connectedness(
  data          = data_strong,
  animal_col    = "animal",
  mu_col        = "MU",
  fixed_formula = ~ 1 + sex,
  sigma2a       = 50,
  sigma2e       = 100,
  relationship  = "Ainv",
  pedigree      = pedigree_strong,
  dry_run       = TRUE
)

diag$mme_dim
diag$schur_W_storage_mb
diag$selected_schur_solver

By default, compute_connectedness() uses the Schur-complement MME solving method (mme_backend = "schur"). The previous full-MME method remains available for validation in small data sets with mme_backend = "full_mme".

With schur_solver = "auto", sparse inverse kernels such as Ainv are routed through CHOLMOD via the Matrix package, whereas dense kernels such as Ginv are routed to a dense compiled solver. If the full dense Schur working matrix Cuu^{-1} Z'X would be too large, "auto" selects "cholmod_lowmem", which constructs the same fixed-effect Schur complement in blocks and solves Cuu^{-1} Z'X b on demand during MU block processing. The "eigen_sparse" option is mainly a diagnostic path for small comparisons.

References

Kennedy, B. W., & Trus, D. (1993). Considerations on genetic connectedness between management units under an animal model. Journal of Animal Science, 71, 2341–2352.

Laloë, D. (1993). Precision and information in linear models of genetic evaluation. Genetics Selection Evolution, 25, 557–576.

Laloë, D., Phocas, F., & Ménissier, F. (1996). Considerations on measures of precision and connectedness in mixed linear models of genetic evaluation. Genetics Selection Evolution, 28, 359–378.

Yu, H., & Morota, G. (2021). GCA: An R package for genetic connectedness analysis using pedigree and genomic data. BMC Genomics, 22, 119.
